actions.justification: ★ MANDATORY: Patient presents with confusion and severe headache, suggesting possible hypertensive encephalopathy or intracranial hemorrhage. Neurological assessment is critical to determine end-organ involvement and guide treatment urgency.

★ MANDATORY: With BP 218/128 and active neurological symptoms, continuous BP monitoring is essential to guide titration of IV antihypertensives and ensure BP is not reduced more than 25% in the first hour (per guideline contraindication).

★ MANDATORY (deadline 30 min): IV antihypertensive must be initiated promptly in hypertensive emergency. Oral-only therapy is contraindicated per guidelines. IV route allows controlled, titratable BP reduction.
MANDATORY per AHA hypertensive emergency guidelines. BMP is required to assess renal function and electrolytes as part of end-organ damage evaluation in hypertensive emergency.
MANDATORY per AHA hypertensive emergency guidelines. Troponin is required to evaluate for cardiac end-organ damage (hypertensive emergency can cause acute coronary syndrome or myocardial injury).

Patient has neurological symptoms (confusion, blurred vision, severe headache) suggestive of hypertensive encephalopathy or other end-organ damage. Formal end-organ damage assessment is required per AHA guidelines and is clinically urgent given the presentation.
Mandatory per AHA guideline for hypertensive crisis assessment within 5 minutes. Patient has severe neurological symptoms and BP 218/128 requiring immediate vital sign assessment.

Mandatory per AHA guideline for hypertensive crisis assessment. Accurate BP measurement in both arms needed to guide IV antihypertensive titration and ensure BP is not reduced more than 25% in first hour.

Patient presents with severe headache, blurred vision, and confusion suggesting hypertensive encephalopathy or other CNS end-organ damage. Neurology consultation is indicated for evaluation and management guidance.

Patient presents with severe headache, blurred vision, and confusion — neurological symptoms requiring urgent CT head to rule out hemorrhagic stroke, hypertensive encephalopathy, or other intracranial pathology as part of end-organ damage assessment.
ECG is indicated to assess for cardiac end-organ damage (LVH, ischemia, arrhythmia) in the context of hypertensive emergency per AHA guidelines.
Chest X-ray to evaluate for pulmonary edema or aortic pathology as part of comprehensive end-organ damage workup in hypertensive emergency.
CBC is needed to evaluate for microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA), thrombocytopenia, and other hematologic complications of hypertensive emergency indicating end-organ damage.
Coagulation studies are needed to assess for DIC and coagulopathy, which can occur with severe hypertensive emergency and end-organ damage.

MRI brain is indicated given neurological symptoms (confusion, headache, blurred vision) to evaluate for hypertensive encephalopathy, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES), or stroke, which would guide treatment targets and urgency.
Assess for renal end-organ damage, which is a critical component of hypertensive emergency evaluation. eGFR helps quantify acute kidney injury.
Urinalysis with microscopy detects proteinuria, hematuria, and casts indicative of hypertensive nephropathy/end-organ damage to the kidneys.
Urine output monitoring is essential to track renal perfusion and detect acute kidney injury in the setting of hypertensive emergency with potential renal end-organ damage.

Patient with hypertensive emergency (BP 218/128, MAP 158) with neurological symptoms (confusion, headache, blurred vision) requires ICU-level continuous monitoring and IV antihypertensive titration after initial assessment and treatment initiation.
